story: Life is never the same all the time. Sometimes, no matter how much good we do or how righteously we live, hardships continue to surround us. Have you ever cried wondering, "Why is this happening only to me?" When people who commit wrongs seem to live comfortably, have you ever felt troubled thinking, "Why am I, despite living honestly, suffering without peace or stability?" Today, we are going to uncover five great secrets hidden behind the Law of Karma—an extraordinary life guide that Lord Krishna gave to Arjuna, and through him, to all of humanity. If you truly understand these secrets, you will gain the power to rewrite your own destiny. Before that, support this effort of spreading Sanatana Dharma and Krishna consciousness. These truths will answer many questions in your life. So, do not skip—listen with complete focus.

Let us enter the story. Long ago, in a kingdom called Avanti, there lived a merchant named Sudhama. Sudhama was not good merely in name but also in character. His business flourished so greatly that people used to say half of the city’s wealth was in his hands. Yet, he never felt pride over his riches. Every morning, after completing his worship, he fed the poor gathered outside his home before eating himself. He never lied, never cheated anyone, and never knowingly harmed even a tiny ant. He was a man of immense virtue.

He lived happily with his wife and two children, and everything seemed to be going well. Just then, fate revealed its cruel nature. One night, due to an unexpected fire accident, all his warehouses were burned to ashes.

The wealth he had accumulated through a lifetime of hard work turned into soot in a single night. Before he could even console himself that at least his life was spared, he discovered that the business partners who had trusted him had betrayed him. His remaining assets were swallowed by creditors. Troubles came one after another like relentless waves. Soon after losing his wealth, a strange disease spread across the city, and Sudhama’s wife and children succumbed to it.

Until yesterday, Sudhama was celebrated as the richest and most charitable man in the city. Now, he was left with nothing—no food to eat, no roof to shelter him, dressed in torn clothes. Those who once received help from him now avoided him. Those who once praised him began accusing him, saying, "He must have committed some grave sin; that is why God punished him."

Sudhama’s heart shattered. Not because he lost his wealth. Not because his loved ones left him. But because the dharma he trusted and the Krishna he worshipped seemed to abandon him in the middle of life’s road. Unable to bear the pain, Sudhama left the city and walked into the forest. He did not know where he was going. He had no footwear, hunger burned inside his stomach, and an even fiercer fire raged in his heart.

Walking endlessly, he entered a dense forest. The terrifying silence and the occasional roars of wild animals did not frighten him—because the storm inside his heart was far more violent than the chaos of nature outside. Exhausted by hunger, he collapsed under a massive banyan tree. He lifted his eyes toward the sky. The sun had already set, and darkness was spreading.

The stars shining in the sky no longer looked like Krishna’s eyes to him. They seemed like the mocking eyes of demons laughing at him. "Krishna!" Sudhama screamed. His voice echoed through the forest. "What wrong have I done? I never harmed anyone. I never hoarded wealth; I fed many people. Then why this fate? Is the law of karma even real? Scriptures say good deeds yield good results and bad deeds yield bad results. Then where did all my goodness go? Why did it turn into ashes? What sin did my wife and children commit that you took them away from me? Do you truly exist, or is all this an illusion?"
Crying uncontrollably, he clutched the tree roots tightly. His tears soaked the ground.

At that moment, Sudhama felt that living itself was meaningless. A life without answers felt heavier than death. He did not know how long he cried or how long he lay unconscious. Slowly, a cool breeze began to blow. It carried a fragrance unlike anything he had known before. It was neither the smell of forest flowers nor soil—it was a divine fragrance that soothed the heart.

Sudhama slowly opened his eyes. Before him, at some distance, a small flame was glowing. In that pitch-dark forest, where did that flame come from? Was someone there? Filled with curiosity, ignoring his weakness, he got up and walked toward the light. As he approached, he noticed a sage sitting calmly.

The sage’s face radiated brilliance. His eyes were closed, as if in deep meditation. The atmosphere around him was profoundly peaceful—so peaceful that even the turbulence inside Sudhama’s heart settled for a moment. Sudhama stood at a short distance, unsure whether to call out.
Just then, without opening his eyes, the sage smiled and said, "Come, Sudhama. I have been waiting for you."

Sudhama felt as though his heart stopped. How could this man know his name? In this forest, at midnight, who was this person who knew him and claimed to be waiting for him? With fear and amazement mixed in his voice, Sudhama asked, "Swami, do you know who I am? How do you know my name?"
The sage slowly opened his eyes. In those eyes, Sudhama saw the depth of an ocean and the vastness of the sky.
The sage said, "My child, not only do I know your name—I know your questions as well. I know why you are crying and whom you are angry with. Sit."
Sudhama sat before him like one hypnotized.

The sage threw a small stick into the fire and said, "Sudhama, you believe that because you are a good person, only good should happen to you. You think that because you performed charity and righteousness, suffering should never come near you. But the law of karma is not a business transaction. It is not a marketplace where you bargain with God saying, 'I gave this, so you give me that.' Karma is subtle, profound, and far more complex than human imagination."

Sudhama felt anger rise within him. "Swami, please don’t speak philosophy. My stomach burns with hunger. My life has turned to ashes. When goodness has no value, why should dharma exist? Why should justice exist? Where is the compassion of that Krishna?" he questioned bitterly.

The sage did not waver in the slightest. He smiled calmly and said, "My child, I will tell you a story. Listen carefully. It is not just a story—it is the secret of creation itself. Once, there lived a sculptor. He took a stone and began chiseling it with his hammer. The stone felt pain and cried, ‘Why are you torturing me? Leave me alone!’ But the sculptor did not stop. He struck harder and harder. The stone felt anger, pain, and hatred—but the sculptor continued his work without pause. Finally, do you know what that stone became?" The sage paused and looked straight into Sudhama’s eyes.

Sudhama remained silent. The sage continued, "That stone became a magnificent idol, worshipped in the sanctum of a temple. If the stone had broken in fear, today it would be lying crushed under people’s feet. Your life is exactly the same, Sudhama."
Sudhama was confused. "What does that mean? Is God’s intention to destroy me? Is taking my wife and children also part of that sculpting? What kind of justice is this, Swami?" he asked.

The sage sighed deeply. "What you are experiencing now is only a small fragment of the whole picture. If someone walks into a movie halfway and says they don’t understand the story, is that fair? In the flow of your many births, this is just a small turning point. If you truly understand the secrets of karma that Sri Krishna explained in the Bhagavathgita, all these questions will melt away like ice. First, you must understand—what is karma? How many types are there? When do the results of our actions manifest? Are we writing our own destiny, or are we merely puppets bound by someone else’s script? Not knowing these truths, humans drown in an ocean of sorrow."

There was an inexplicable attraction in the sage’s words. Sudhama’s anger slowly subsided, and curiosity began to rise. "Swami, then please tell me those secrets. Even if not for this life, they may help me in another. I need to know why my destiny is written this way. What are the five secrets Krishna revealed?" he asked.

The sage smiled gently and nodded. "I will tell you, Sudhama. But this is not merely about listening—you must absorb and realize them. The first secret is the justice of karma: only the seed you sow will sprout. You cannot plant a neem seed and expect sweet mangoes. Yet this is where most people stumble."

"People ask, ‘We did not plant neem seeds in this life—then why are we suffering bitter experiences?’ That is where the true secret lies," the sage continued. "Sudhama, every soul carries three bags of karma. The first is Sanchita Karma, the second is Prarabdha Karma, and the third is Agami Karma. These terms may sound new to you, but your entire life revolves around them."

"Sanchita Karma is the accumulated storehouse of merits and sins from your countless past births. It is like a massive warehouse containing all your good and bad deeds. They remain stored there. The second is Prarabdha Karma. From that vast warehouse, God selects a small bundle for you to experience in this present birth. Your wife, children, wealth, suffering, happiness, illnesses—all come from this Prarabdha Karma bag. No matter how virtuous you are in this life, you must experience what is in it."

"It is like an arrow already released from a bow—you cannot pull it back. Sudhama felt that he was beginning to understand, but he was not fully satisfied. He asked, ‘Swami, does that mean my present suffering is only because of sins from my past lives? Then were all my charities and prayers in this life useless? If Prarabdha must be experienced no matter what, why should we worship God or do good deeds at all?’"

This doubt tormented him deeply. The sage laughed softly. "You have asked an excellent question, Sudhama. This is exactly where the third type of karma—Agami Karma—comes into play. Here is where Sri Krishna gives humanity a tremendous opportunity."

"Prarabdha is the debt of the past, but Agami is the cheque you are writing right now for the future. How you respond in this very moment decides what you will face ahead. For example, due to Prarabdha, you may feel hunger today and have no food. That is not in your control. But whether you curse God while starving, or share the handful of grains you have with someone else—that choice is in your hands. That choice creates Agami Karma."

"How a person behaves when suffering arrives—that alone rewrites destiny. Your suffering is like fire meant to melt your Prarabdha. In that fire, will you burn to ashes, or will you shine like purified gold? That is entirely your choice."
As Sudhama listened, he felt an unknown current flow through his body. "Swami, does that mean I can change my suffering? Can I rewrite my destiny?" he asked eagerly.

The sage looked into his eyes sharply and said, "Absolutely. Sri Krishna has shown paths to do so. Though Prarabdha cannot be erased completely, its intensity can be reduced through Karma Yoga. Imagine a massive boulder destined to fall on you—that is your karma. But through merit and divine grace, that boulder may shrink into a small stone that only injures your foot. Pain comes, blood flows—but life remains. This is the true magic hidden within the law of karma."

"However, to achieve this, you must deeply understand five secrets. The first is performing action without attachment to results. It sounds simple, but practicing it is like walking on the edge of a sword."

Sudhama fell into deep thought. "How is it possible to work without expecting results? Every human works with some expectation, doesn’t he?" he wondered. Indeed, even he had performed charity expecting merit, heaven, or God’s favor. Realizing this, he felt ashamed. Did his devotion also contain selfishness? Was his faith also a transaction? The sage observed the changing expressions on Sudhama’s face and said, "Do you see, Sudhama? Your own conscience is questioning you. Behind every action lies a subtle thought—‘What do I gain from this?’ That very thought binds us in karmic chains."

"Krishna told Arjuna the same truth: ‘Karmanye vadhikaraste, ma phaleshu kadachana.’ You have the right only to action, not to its results. But we often misunderstand this teaching," the sage continued.

Sudhama asked, "If we do not think about results, how will we work with dedication?" The sage smiled and said, "This is where Krishna revealed a powerful technique—the concept of Yajna. Yajna does not mean rituals or fire sacrifices alone. Yajna means sacrifice. Yajna means offering."

"Whatever you do—eating, walking, doing business—perform it as an offering to God, as worship. A soldier gives his life for his country because it is his duty, not for reward. Similarly, fulfill your responsibilities as a father, husband, or citizen without calculating gain or loss. When you surrender the results to God, the merit and sin of those results no longer cling to you."
"Just as water does not stick to a lotus leaf, you can live in the world without being bound by karma. This is the first step of Karma Yoga."

The sage’s words penetrated deep into Sudhama’s heart. He felt as though a great burden he had been carrying for years was slowly lifting. Yet many questions still remained. "Swami, what you say is noble, but in practice it is extremely difficult. When someone wrongs us, anger naturally arises. When we lose hard-earned wealth, sorrow is inevitable. How can we conquer these emotions? How can I accept the death of my wife and children as Krishna’s grace? How can I attain such equanimity?" Sudhama asked, tears flowing from his eyes.

At that moment, the sage stood up. In the glow of the fire, his form appeared even more radiant. "Sudhama," he said, "to conquer emotions and burn karma completely, Krishna revealed another secret—the second secret. It is so powerful that even fear of death vanishes once you understand it."

"To understand this secret, you must first witness a vision. This is no ordinary vision—it is an event from your past life." Saying this, the sage took water from his kamandalu and sprinkled it over Sudhama’s eyes.

Instantly, the forest vanished. Sudhama found himself standing on a battlefield. Trumpeting elephants, galloping horses, and the cries of soldiers filled the air. A sword was in his hand, and his body was covered in bloodstains. At his feet lay a man. That man was none other than the very business partner who had betrayed him in this life.

Sudhama was speechless. What was happening? Why was he about to kill this man? Suddenly, an arrow flew and pierced Sudhama’s chest. The one who shot the arrow was none other than the woman who was his wife in this present life.

Sudhama staggered back screaming, "No!" The vision vanished, and the forest returned. Gasping and drenched in sweat, he looked at the sage. "Swami, was what I saw real? Did my wife kill me? Was my partner my enemy?" he asked, trembling.

The sage replied gravely, "Yes, Sudhama. Without debt there is no birth; without relationship there is no bond. The betrayal you experienced in this life is merely the settlement of accounts from a past life. The balance was settled. But the real secret lies elsewhere."
"Before you died in that battlefield, do you know what the final thought in your mind was? That thought alone determined your present birth."
Sudhama held his breath. "Please tell me, Swami—what is that secret?" he asked.

The sage stepped forward. Sudhama stood frozen in the firelight. His heart raced. The battlefield vision replayed in his mind—the arrow, the enemy, and most of all, the face of the one who shot him: his wife.
How could anyone digest such a truth? The woman who loved him in this life was the one who killed him in the previous one. Fear and confusion replaced his anger toward God.

Trembling, Sudhama cried, "Is this real, or is it an illusion? Was my wife—mother of my children—my killer? Is the line between love and hatred truly so thin? Was her love in this life merely an act? Swami, please tell me—I am losing my sanity."

The sage approached him, placed a hand on his shoulder, and seated him upright. In that touch was the compassion of a mother and the assurance of a father. "Calm yourself, Sudhama. Truth is always bitter, but within that bitterness lies the power to cure. What you saw was not illusion—it was a memory buried within your soul."

"Now answer my question. When the arrow pierced your heart and your life was slipping away, what was the thought in your mind? Look within and remember. What was your final thought?" the sage asked, staring directly into his eyes.

Sudhama closed his eyes. The scene replayed vividly. Blood flowed. Rage burned within him. Suddenly, the memory became clear. Opening his eyes, he said, "Swami, in that moment I was consumed by intense hatred. I thought, ‘I will not spare you. Wherever you go, I will follow you. I will settle this debt.’ That was my final thought."

The sage smiled. "That, my child, is the secret. Krishna revealed this supreme principle in the Gita: ‘Yam yam vapi smaran bhavam tyajaty ante kalevaram.’ Whatever state of mind a person holds at the time of death, that alone determines the destination of the next birth."

"You vowed that you would not let go, that you would pursue and settle the debt. That resolve was so powerful it commanded nature itself. Your hatred and urge to repay that debt brought you together again in this life. But karma does not always respond sword with sword. It works in mysterious ways. Enemies in one life are often born as the closest relations in another—husband and wife, parent and child. Do you know why? Love and hatred are both chains that bind the soul. Whether iron or gold, a chain is still a chain. Your enemy was born as your wife in this life. The one who took your life in the previous birth served you, loved you, and finally repaid that old debt through devotion and sacrifice."
Sudhama felt his throat tighten. "Then was what existed between us not love at all? Was it merely a transaction? Once the debt was repaid, did she leave?" he asked in anguish.

The sage nodded. "This is what is called Rinanubandha—bondage through debt. ‘Rinanubandha rupena pashu patni suta alayah’—wife, children, wealth, and possessions come into our lives only to settle debts from past births. Anyone who enters your life must either give something to you or take something from you. Once the transaction is complete, destiny separates you."

"You are crying because your wife died. But from the standpoint of karma, she has fully repaid her debt and departed liberated. She served you, gave you happiness, and finally attained freedom. In truth, you should feel joy that a soul has unburdened itself. But illusion blinds the eyes and makes you weep, clinging to ‘my wife’ and ‘my children.’"

"Life is like a train journey. Some people sit beside us, converse for a while, and then get down at their station. Do we cry because they leave? No. Life is the same—when someone’s station arrives, they depart. You are still on the journey."

As Sudhama listened, the weight in his heart felt as though it was being lifted by unseen hands. Until now, he believed injustice had been done to him. But now, understanding that what had to happen had happened, his suffering began to seem meaningless.

Yet another doubt lingered. "Swami, what you say may be true. But humans are emotional beings. How can I forget my losses? Let us assume my family’s debts are settled. But what about my friends who cheated me and took my wealth? Does that mean I cheated them in a past life, and now they are collecting their dues?"

The sage burst into laughter, his voice echoing through the forest. "Excellent question, Sudhama! You have grasped the core of the knot. If you took their wealth in a past life, then now they have taken it back—the account is settled. You should rejoice. But if you never took anything from them and yet they cheated you, then they are now indebted to you. That means, with interest, they must return it in the future. Either way, dharma always prevails."

"But here lies the real danger. They cheated you—that is their karma. But if you now nurture hatred, curse them, or seek revenge, you are creating fresh karma. That is Agami Karma. In the fire meant to burn your accumulated karma, you are throwing in new garbage. The fire does not diminish—it grows stronger."
"That is why Krishna said that forgiving—even tolerating—the one who harmed you is itself a form of yoga."

Sudhama pondered deeply. "Swami, this sounds beautiful, but in practice it feels impossible. I have lost everything. How can I behave as though nothing happened? Is there no way to permanently escape these karmic bonds? I do not want to be reborn. I do not want another wife, another enemy, another betrayal. Please tell me the secret to break free from this cycle."

The sage lifted him gently and said, "There is, Sudhama. That is the third secret. It is extremely subtle. If you understand it, you will remain the same whether you live as a king or a beggar. Its name is Akartṛtva Bhava—the sense of non-doership. But before I explain it, you must undergo a small test."

"You are thirsty, aren’t you?" the sage asked. Sudhama realized his throat was dry. "Yes, Swami," he replied. The sage pointed to a small earthen pot filled with water. "Go and drink. But on one condition—while drinking, you must feel that it is not you who is drinking the water."

Sudhama found the request strange. "I am the one drinking—how can I think it is not me?" Still, he agreed to try. He lifted the pot, brought it to his lips, and drank. Cool water flowed down his throat, reviving him. Instantly he thought, ‘Ah, how refreshing!’
The sage’s voice thundered, "Stop! You have failed." Startled, Sudhama lowered the pot. "What happened, Swami? I had not even finished drinking," he protested.

The sage said calmly, "I asked you to drink without the sense of ‘I’. But your mind said, ‘I am drinking. I feel relief.’ That ‘I’—the ego—is what binds you. ‘I donated, I worshipped, I did business, I raised a family.’ This ‘I’ is the real thief."

"Krishna told Arjuna the same truth: ‘Gunā guneshū vartante’—the qualities of nature perform their actions. The Self is merely the witness. The body drank the water. The breath was satisfied. The mind experienced relief. Where were you—the soul? You were only observing."
"The moment you abandon the notion ‘I am the doer,’ karma no longer clings to you."

"Even if a person commits violence, if he truly knows ‘I am not the doer; nature acts through me,’ then the sin does not bind him. But reaching that state is not easy," the sage said. Sudhama felt dizzy. "Swami, if this body is mine, and actions happen through it, then who else is acting if not me? When I give charity with my own hands, how does the merit not come to me? When I commit a sin, how does the punishment not fall upon me?" he asked.

The sage smiled. "This is a natural doubt. Listen to an example. A lamp is burning. In its light, one man reads the Bhagavatam, while another writes a forged letter. The same light enables both good and bad acts. Do the sins or merits stick to the lamp? No. Because the lamp is merely a witness. It illuminates, but it does not act."

"Similarly, the soul within you is like that lamp. Your body and mind are instruments operating in that light. If you remain established as the witnessing soul, karma does not bind you. But when you identify as the body and say, ‘I am doing this,’ karma stains you."

"Your charitable acts gave you merit—this is true. But that very merit becomes golden chains. It takes you to heaven, gives pleasure, and once that pleasure is exhausted, throws you back to earth. Merit too is bondage. Moksha is a state beyond both sin and merit. This is the essence of Nishkama Karma that Krishna taught."
Sudhama looked up at the sky. He realized how ignorant he had been. He believed that doing good was enough, never realizing that ego hidden behind goodness was also dangerous.

"Swami, intellectually I understand that ‘I am not this body; I am the witness.’ But in practice, when hunger strikes or pain arises, the ‘I’ returns immediately. Is there any method to overcome this?" Sudhama asked.

The sage smiled. "Yes—through constant practice. Offer every action to Krishna and see yourself as a mere instrument. Imagine a flute. It is hollow, empty of ego. That is why Krishna can produce divine music through it. If the flute thinks, ‘I am playing,’ the music collapses into noise. You must become like that flute."
"When the feeling ‘I am nothing; He is everything’ becomes natural, surrender is born. Then every action performed through you becomes divine service."
As the sage spoke, Sudhama felt a deep calm descend upon his mind. But the journey was not yet complete. Suddenly, the sage’s expression grew serious.

"Sudhama, understanding non-doership is only the beginning. The real challenge is this: I told you that the results of karma are not in our hands. Yet sometimes, even when we commit no wrongdoing, the world condemns us. Even great souls like Sita were slandered. Even devotees like Draupadi were humiliated. If such virtuous beings suffered, how can ordinary people like us endure social blame and injustice? Should we simply remain silent, calling it karma?"
"The answer lies in Krishna’s fourth secret. But to grasp it, you must face a terrifying truth."
Sudhama looked at him in shock. "More terrifying than seeing my wife kill me in a past life? What could be worse than that, Swami?"

The sage smiled—but his smile carried a warning. "Yes, Sudhama. The enemy within is far more dangerous than the enemy outside. What I will now show you is not your past—but your future. Yes, you heard correctly. I will show you an event that will occur in your future."
"Beyond this forest lies a city. Tomorrow morning, you will face an experience there—one that will transform your life forever. Do you wish to see it, or will you stop here?"

Sudhama’s heart began to race. Knowing the future is dangerous. If known, peace vanishes; if unknown, preparation is impossible. After a moment of resolve, Sudhama said firmly, "Swami, I am ready. Show me what will happen tomorrow. Tell me the fourth secret."
The sage took water from his kamandalu and began chanting again. This time, the color of the flames changed. Red flames slowly turned blue. Within the fire, a vision began to move.
Seeing it, Sudhama stepped back in terror. "Is that… me? Why am I doing that?" he screamed. In the vision, Sudhama appeared dressed as a king, holding a sword, about to kill an infant.
"Swami! What is this horror? Am I killing a baby? Is there any sin greater than this? Why would karma turn me into such a monster?" Sudhama trembled violently.

The sage gripped his shoulder firmly. "Do not panic. You have only seen the surface. Who that child is, why you are about to kill him, and the subtle dharma behind it—once you understand these, your reverence for karma will increase a thousandfold. This is not merely murder. It is liberation."

"This is the fourth secret—the battle between karma and dharma. Sometimes, for the sake of dharma, karma itself must be used as a weapon. Krishna explained this truth. You will understand it tomorrow. But for that, we must now begin a journey. Are you ready?"
Wiping sweat from his face, Sudhama nodded, caught in a trance. He followed the sage into the dark forest, driven by an intense desire to uncover the remaining secrets that would change his destiny.

The night promised to reveal even more secrets. The longing to understand the five principles that could rewrite his destiny kept Sudhama moving forward. As the sage walked ahead, Sudhama followed him through the dark forest.

Greetings. Our journey has paused at a deeply intense turning point. Sudhama has just witnessed a terrifying vision of his future—himself raising a sword to kill an infant—and is shaken to his core. Why would a good, God-fearing man commit such a cruel act? What is the karmic secret behind it? In this third phase, what we are about to uncover is not just an answer, but one of the most complex principles that Sri Krishna taught Arjuna on the battlefield of Kurukshetra. Understanding this will give you the power to discern right from wrong in your own life. Before we proceed, remember to like this video and subscribe to our channel.

Listen to this narration till the end, because the trial Sudhama is about to face will confront you too at some point in your life. Sudhama continues to walk behind the sage, but his legs tremble. The vision keeps replaying in his mind.

"Swami, please stop. I am exhausted. I am terrified. Why must I kill that infant? What kind of dharma is this? Why would God turn me into such a demon? Please reveal the fourth secret and clear my confusion," Sudhama pleaded, breaking down.
The sage sat upon a large rock and motioned for Sudhama to sit beside him. Breaking the forest silence, the sage began speaking in a deep, steady voice.

"Sudhama, what you saw was only the surface. You do not yet know the intention behind it. That hidden intention is the fourth and most crucial secret within the law of karma. Its name is Karmagati or Dharma Sukshma—the subtlety of dharma. Sri Krishna said in the Bhagavathgita, ‘Gahana karmano gatih,’ meaning the path of karma is extremely deep and difficult to comprehend."
"What appears to be dharma on the surface may be adharma. What appears to be adharma may be supreme dharma."
Sudhama was still confused. "Does that mean killing can also be dharma? How can killing an infant become virtue, Swami?" he asked innocently.

The sage smiled gently. "Listen carefully. In the future vision you saw, that infant is not an ordinary child. He is a carrier of a deadly poison. If he lives, before he grows into adulthood, the entire kingdom will perish in a devastating plague. Hundreds of thousands of innocent people will die. Only you will know this truth."

"At that moment, as a king, what is your dharma? Should you spare one child out of compassion and become the cause of mass death? Or should you sacrifice one life to save millions? There, you raise the sword not out of hatred, not out of cruelty, but solely to protect countless lives."
"For the welfare of the world, that act is not sin—it is liberation. Even for that soul, it is a blessing, because you prevent him from becoming the cause of unimaginable destruction."
As Sudhama listened, a flash of understanding crossed his mind. "So intention matters more than the act itself?" he asked.

"Exactly," the sage praised him. "A doctor cuts open a patient’s body with a knife. A thief stabs a traveler with a knife. The action is the same—blood flows, pain occurs. But we honor the doctor and imprison the thief. Why? Because the doctor’s intention is to save life, while the thief’s intention is to take it."

"Krishna judges not your hands, but your heart. If your intention is pure, even the hardest action performed for dharma becomes yoga. That is the equanimity of Karma Yoga. On the battlefield of Kurukshetra, when Arjuna hesitated to fight his own kin, Krishna taught him this same truth."

Sudhama sighed deeply. "Swami, this principle is profound. But how does it relate to my life? I never cheated anyone in business. My intention was always good. Then why did such suffering come to me? My partners cheated me with evil intent—yet they seem to live comfortably. Why hasn’t karma punished them?"

The sage looked at him compassionately. "Sudhama, you are still looking at the outer world. Who told you they are at peace? Just because they smile does not mean their hearts are calm. A wrongdoer begins living in fear the moment he commits the act—fear of exposure, fear of loss. That inner fear itself is hell."
"External wealth never gives peace. The greatest punishment is the absence of inner peace."
"Then what about my losses? I had good intentions," Sudhama protested.

"This is where you must truly understand the fourth secret," the sage replied. "Sometimes God gives us suffering not to punish us, but to protect us. Yes—your wealth is gone. Your family is gone. It feels like punishment. But had the wealth remained, perhaps arrogance would have blinded you and driven you toward greater sins. Or perhaps God took your wife and children away to protect them from a greater calamity."

"A mother forces her child to drink bitter medicine. The child cries and hits her, but the mother knows it will save the child’s life. What happened to you is the bitter medicine Krishna gave you—to remove your ignorance and ego. You see it as punishment, but it is protection. Humans curse God only because they do not understand this."
Tears filled Sudhama’s eyes. For so long, he had seen himself as a victim. Now, the thought that everything might have happened for his own good filled him with a strange new hope.
Sudhama wiped his tears. "Swami, does that mean all my suffering was meant for my purification? Just as gold is heated in fire only to shine brighter—am I in that stage now?" he asked.

The sage nodded. "Yes. You are now ready. Your anger has reduced, hatred has softened, questions have diminished, and acceptance has grown. This itself is spiritual progress. Now we are approaching the fifth and final secret. But before that, one last test awaits you."

"Beyond this forest lies a city. There, you will encounter a man. The moment you see him, your blood will boil. All your past hatred will awaken at once. What you choose to do in that moment will determine your future," the sage said.

As they walked, dawn began to break. Sunlight filtered through the forest trees. They crossed the forest boundary and reached the outskirts of a small village. There stood a dilapidated temple. "Let us rest here for a while," said the sage.
Exhausted, Sudhama sat on the temple steps. "Swami, who is that man? Why would anger arise in me now? I feel I have no hatred left," he said confidently.
The sage smiled. "We shall see whether your wisdom stands firm or whether your ego wins when the moment arrives."

Just then, in the distance, an old man appeared, walking with the help of a stick. His clothes were torn. His body was covered with sores, swarmed by flies. He struggled with every step, moving toward the temple.
His throat parched with thirst, the old man cried out weakly, "Water, child… please give me some water. It will be a great merit."

Sudhama felt compassion rise within him. He had water in the pot beside him. He stood up to give it. But as the old man came closer, Sudhama froze. The pot slipped from his hands and shattered on the ground.

Sudhama’s eyes turned red with rage. His body trembled violently. Because that old man was none other than Veerabhadra—the chief business partner who had betrayed him, destroyed his life, and left him on the streets.

All the past replayed in Sudhama’s mind like a reel—Veerabhadra gaining his trust, taking his signatures, burning the warehouses, and laughing when Sudhama was ruined. Now the same Veerabhadra, afflicted with leprosy, stood helpless before him, awaiting death.
A demon awakened within Sudhama. "So you are here, thief! After destroying my life, you come to me for water? Even if I kill you, it would not be a sin," his mind screamed.
"No—killing is not enough. I should let you die slowly of thirst and enjoy my revenge," he thought. He picked up a stone lying nearby.
The sage watched silently, without intervening. Sudhama raised the stone. Veerabhadra lifted his eyes and recognized him. There was no fear in them—only remorse.

"Sudhama, are you God? Has God sent me to you? Kill me, Sudhama. Kill me. This disease is not enough punishment for my sins. Only if I die by your hands will I find liberation," Veerabhadra pleaded, falling at Sudhama’s feet.
The stone trembled in Sudhama’s hand. On one side burned vengeance; on the other echoed the sage’s teachings on subtle dharma. His mind was torn apart.
"He is my enemy. Punishing him is my duty. Krishna himself said that the wicked must be punished," his mind argued.

At that moment, the sage’s voice rang out. "Sudhama, stop. This is your final test. If you throw that stone, you will be trapped again in the cycle of karma. He is already suffering the result of his deeds. Karma never spares anyone."

"But your response right now will shape your future. To know the fifth secret Krishna revealed, you must make a choice. You may think forgiveness is the weapon—but there is something even greater. It is the sword that cuts karma at its very root. Will you wield that sword, or will you throw this stone?"
Sudhama stood frozen in conflict. The stone felt unbearably heavy. "Swami, how can I forgive him? He indirectly caused the death of my wife and children," Sudhama cried.

The sage stepped closer and whispered into his ear, "Sudhama, this man is none other than your father from a past life—the father who protected you like his own eyes. To repay that debt, he took your wealth in this life. But he strayed and committed sin. Now tell me—will you kill your father? Or will you deny water to a thirsty father and send him to hell?"
Sudhama felt as if his heart stopped. The stone slipped from his hand and fell to the ground. The word ‘Father’ choked his throat. Tears flooded his eyes.
Seeing an enemy as a father… recognizing a relative within a betrayer—was this the wonder of karma? Sudhama collapsed, sobbing, and embraced Veerabhadra.
Veerabhadra did not understand what was happening. Sudhama took the sage’s kamandalu and poured water into Veerabhadra’s mouth.
As Veerabhadra drank, life returned to his eyes. The hatred vanished from Sudhama’s face, replaced by a divine radiance.

The sage smiled and clapped his hands. "Magnificent, Sudhama. You have passed. You are now worthy of learning the most secret and powerful fifth truth of karma. Once you know it, there will be no birth, no death, no suffering. You will merge with Krishna himself."

"But to learn this secret, you must now perform a physical act. Inside this temple’s sanctum lies an idol—not an ordinary one. You must look into its eyes and ask a question. Remember—the idol will not speak. Your heart will answer."
Wiping his tears, Sudhama said, "I will go, Swami. Tell me—what is the fifth secret? Untie the final knot."
The sage gazed at the sky. "The time has come. Enter the sanctum. What you will see there is not an idol—it is your own true Self. But beware—there is someone else inside."

Sudhama stepped into the temple sanctum. Darkness surrounded him. A strange fragrance filled the air—neither pure sandalwood nor tulsi, yet deeply sacred and calming. The doors of the sanctum were half open. As his eyes adjusted to the dim light, he looked inside.

What he saw made him freeze in shock. There was no idol. No image of God. In the center of the sanctum stood a tall mirror—unlike any ordinary mirror. Ancient carvings decorated its borders, but at its center swirled a dark, rotating void.

Sudhama stood before it in confusion. "Swami, what is this? Where is the idol? Whom am I supposed to ask?" he shouted. But there was no reply from outside. The silence of the sanctum rang in his ears.
Just as he turned back in disappointment, the mirror began to stir. The dark vortex slowly parted, and an image emerged within it.
Sudhama assumed it was his own reflection. But to his astonishment, the image was not his. It was the sage who had been guiding him.
Fear gripped him. "How is this possible? I am standing before the mirror—how can the sage’s reflection appear inside it?"
The reflection smiled. In that smile was the brilliance of a thousand suns. A deep, resonant voice echoed from within the mirror.
"Sudhama, the God you are searching for does not exist outside you. He resides within. Until now, you have only seen my illusionary form. What you are seeing now is the truth."

"I am not separate from you, and you are not separate from me. What stands between this realization and you is only your karma. I brought you here to reveal the fifth and final secret—the one that burns karma completely."

Sudhama’s entire body trembled. "So the sage who walked with me was not ordinary? Swami, what is this fifth secret? How can I permanently erase my sins and merits? I am exhausted. I want liberation from this cycle of birth and death," he pleaded, kneeling before the mirror.

The voice spoke gently. "Listen carefully. The first four secrets—selfless action, remembrance at death, non-doership, and protection of dharma—are paths to loosen karmic bonds. But even after mastering them, a subtle ego may remain."

"The ego that says, ‘I am practicing Nishkama Karma,’ is itself bondage. Even golden chains bind the feet. That is why Krishna revealed the ultimate secret—the fifth secret—Sharanagati: complete surrender."
Sudhama asked innocently, "Swami, does surrender mean ritual worship or offering prayers?"

The voice replied, "No, my child. Sharanagati means merging your will completely with the will of the Supreme. Krishna said in the Gita: ‘Sarva dharman parityajya mam ekam sharanam vraja’—abandon all calculations of right and wrong, merit and sin, and surrender solely unto Me. I will liberate you from all sins."
"This sounds simple, but it is the hardest path. Humans trust their own effort more than God. Surrender does not mean irresponsibility—it is the highest form of love."

"Imagine a small child holding his father’s finger in a crowded fair. The child does not know the path, but he feels no fear because his father’s hand holds him. If the child lets go and says, ‘I will walk on my own,’ he will be lost."

"Life is the same fair. Karma is the crowd. You cannot conquer it with your strength or intelligence. The mountain of accumulated karma cannot be cleared by a single lifetime of effort. That is why surrender alone dissolves karma."
"The moment you say, ‘Krishna, my strength is insufficient, my intelligence is insufficient, my life is Yours,’ and accept both suffering and joy as His grace, your karmic ledger is torn apart."
Sudhama listened as if struck by lightning. "Swami, does that mean all my past sins and merits vanish? But you said karma must be experienced."

The voice answered, "Under normal law, yes. Just as a citizen must obey the law. But if you become the king’s own beloved, can the king not pardon you? Karma is My law. Bhakti and surrender are My love. Love transcends law."

"When you become completely Mine, karma itself fears to touch you. Just as no animal dares attack when you stand beside a lion, no planet, fate, curse, or sin can harm one who stands in Krishna’s refuge."

Sudhama trembled and asked, "Swami, am I worthy of such surrender? Until yesterday, I blamed God. I cried out of attachment to my wife and children. I wanted to kill my enemy. With such an impure heart, will He accept me?"

At once, the radiance within the mirror intensified. The voice replied, "Sudhama, when trash or fragrant wood is placed in fire, both turn to ash. Fire never discriminates saying, ‘I will burn only the good, not the bad.’ Krishna’s name is that fire. No matter how sinful a person is, if he calls Krishna even once with a sincere heart, he is purified."

"Valmiki was once a violent criminal, yet by chanting Rama’s name he became a sage. Ajamila was a great sinner, yet was liberated by uttering Narayana’s name. God does not look at your past deeds—He looks only at the intensity of your cry."

"You have repentance—that itself is the first qualification. You gave water to your enemy just now. That single act is your ticket. The moment you killed the idea of ‘mine’ and saw God even in your enemy, you became ready for surrender."

Sudhama folded his hands. "Swami, I understand now. I have no desires left in life. I do not grieve for lost wealth or departed loved ones. I see them all as forms of You. I surrender my entire life at Your feet. Do with me as You wish."

Closing his eyes, Sudhama surrendered completely. At that moment, he felt an indescribable experience. His body felt light, as if floating. The heavy stone that had pressed upon his heart for years dissolved. A boundless peace and bliss flooded his being. He laughed aloud—not in madness, but in supreme joy.
Suddenly, the mirror vanished. Silence returned to the sanctum. But within that silence, a new presence emerged—from behind him.
Sudhama turned around. There stood the sage—but now transformed. In his hands was a flute. A peacock feather adorned his crown. His smile held the charm of all three worlds.
Sudhama gasped, overwhelmed with joy and awe. "Krishna… is it You? Were You the one who walked with me all along?" he whispered.

The divine form smiled and said, "Yes, Sudhama. Your suffering did not come because I was far from you. It came because I wanted to pull you closer to Me. When you had wealth, you were generous—but not devoted. Ego lived within you. To break that ego, I used suffering as purification."

"You did not break—you transformed into a beautiful sculpture. You learned the five secrets of karma: renunciation of results, remembrance at death, non-doership, protection of dharma, and complete surrender. You are now a Jivanmukta—liberated while alive."
Sudhama fell at Krishna’s feet and cried, "Lord, I have no need for this world anymore. Take me with You. Do not send me back among deception and suffering. I cannot bear it."
Krishna gently lifted him. "This desire is common among devotees. Once wisdom dawns, detachment from the world arises. But my plan is different."
"Even Arjuna wanted to abandon the battlefield and retreat to the forest—but I did not allow it. One who has attained knowledge must not escape. He must live it and demonstrate it for the world."

"You are liberated, yes—but your Prarabdha karma still remains. Your body has not fallen yet. A responsibility awaits you beyond this forest. Do you remember the future vision you saw—the infant and the sword? That moment will arrive tomorrow."
"If it does not unfold properly, a terrible calamity will strike. But now you possess a new weapon. Not a sword. With this weapon, you can stop that disaster without killing the child."
Sudhama was astonished. "Without killing the child? Is that possible? Can destiny be changed?"
Krishna laughed playfully. "Karma writes destiny, but Karma Yoga can rewrite it. If you fully understand the fifth secret, even death can be transformed into life."

"Tomorrow morning, you will enter the city. The king will have died without an heir. According to tradition, the royal elephant will roam the streets with a garland. Whose neck it chooses—he will become king."

"The elephant will choose you. You will ascend the throne. Then the infant will be brought before you. At that moment, what will you do? Will you act with old wisdom and kill him? Or will you create a new path through surrender? That is your final test."
"Go now, Sudhama. The world is waiting for you. Remember—if you sit upon the throne, do not forget: it is not you who sits there. It is I who sit through you."
With these words, the divine form slowly dissolved. Sudhama was left alone in the dark sanctum—but the darkness no longer frightened him. His heart shone with a thousand volts of light.

He rose. His walk carried royal dignity. The beggar who had entered the temple now walked out like an emperor. Yet the challenge ahead was immense. Would he truly become king? Who was that infant? How would he stop the calamity without killing? All would be revealed at dawn.

Sudhama stepped out of the temple. Veerabhadra was still lying unconscious outside. Sudhama looked at him and smiled. "Rise, my friend. Our journey is not over yet. Tomorrow, we will create a new history," he said. As he looked toward the sky, the sun was rising—not merely a new day, but the dawn of Sudhama’s new life.

But destiny had one final twist hidden at its last turn. Greetings. This is the final chapter of our journey. A simple merchant who lost everything, understood the deepest secrets of karma, and transformed into a yogi—Sudhama’s story is reaching its conclusion. Yet the ending holds an unexpected turn. Did Sudhama truly change destiny by following Krishna’s five secrets? Did he save the kingdom without killing the child? Let us find out.

Sudhama, with Veerabhadra behind him, entered the city. A strange silence hung over the streets. Anxiety was visible on the faces of the people. Upon inquiry, Sudhama learned that the king had died of a heart attack the previous night. The king had no heir, and the kingdom was in turmoil.

According to ancient tradition, the royal priests had released the coronation elephant into the city, carrying a garland. Whomever the elephant chose would become the next king—believed to be divine will.

Just as Sudhama stepped into the royal street, the elephant approached with majestic calm. Thousands of people watched with held breath. Sudhama stood detached, as a silent witness, with no desire or fear—only surrender to Krishna’s will.

The elephant walked past everyone and stopped before Sudhama, who was dressed in torn clothes. People gasped in disbelief. But the elephant looked into Sudhama’s eyes, recognized the radiance of his awakened soul, bowed its head, and placed the garland around his neck, trumpeting loudly.

The crowd erupted in cheers. The royal priests rushed forward and bowed at Sudhama’s feet. The man who had no food yesterday now sat upon the throne. Yet there was no pride on his face—only the awareness that Krishna was seated through him.
At that moment, Veerabhadra approached and sought permission to serve Sudhama as a minister. Sudhama smiled and accepted. Everything seemed to fall into harmony.

Suddenly, the royal priests rushed into the court. Behind them came a woman, crying, holding an infant in her arms. Trembling, the chief priest spoke, "Maharaja, our astrological calculations reveal a terrifying truth. This child is no ordinary being. According to the scriptures, he is a bearer of deadly poison. If he remains alive, by tomorrow’s sunrise a devastating plague will wipe out the entire kingdom."
"To save millions, the child must be sacrificed immediately. This is Rajadharma," the priests declared.

Sudhama’s heart sank. This was the vision he had seen in the fire. Ministers and priests urged him to act without delay. The mother fell at his feet, begging him to spare her child and exile them instead.

Sudhama descended from the throne. A sword was placed in his hand. This was the moment of trial. With intellect alone, the child must be killed. That was the fourth secret—dharma protection. But with the heart, the fifth secret called him—surrender through love.

Sudhama closed his eyes. "Krishna, You said love alone can conquer karma. I saw myself killing this child in the forest. Today, I choose to rewrite that destiny. Whatever the consequence—sin or curse—I will not kill this child. I place everything at Your feet," he prayed.

Sudhama threw the sword to the ground. The sound echoed through the court. Silence followed. He lifted the infant into his arms. The child’s body was dark, toxic, and burning with poison. Yet Sudhama did not recoil.
Holding the child tightly to his chest, Sudhama prayed, "Krishna, if this poison is meant for this kingdom, let it enter me instead. Protect this child and these people."

A miracle occurred. Dark smoke began to rise from the infant and enter Sudhama’s body. The people screamed in terror. Sudhama’s body trembled and darkened, as though absorbing death itself—like Shiva swallowing poison.
At that instant, the fire of surrender within Sudhama blazed fiercely. The poison could not withstand the Krishna-consciousness within him. It burned away into nothingness.
Moments later, the darkness vanished. Sudhama stood radiant, glowing a thousand times brighter. The infant transformed—his skin turned golden, and he laughed joyfully.
The priests stood stunned. "This is impossible! How can destiny be false?" they cried.

A divine voice echoed from the sky: "The child was indeed born carrying poison as per karma. But when a selfless yogi, free of ego and filled with surrender, absorbs karma with love, even destiny bows. Love alone can burn karma. Sudhama used love, not the sword. Therefore, he did not merely become king—he became divine."

The final revelation was this: the child was the embodied result of Sudhama’s past charity—a test, not a curse. Because Sudhama passed, the child grew up to rule the kingdom after him, creating a reign like Rama Rajya.
Sudhama ruled for many years—not as a king, but as a servant of Krishna. He never thought, ‘I am the ruler.’ He governed as a representative of the Divine.
When the time came, Sudhama smiled, shed his body, and attained Vaikuntha—eternal liberation.

Do you see now? Destiny is not a stone—it is clay. The five secrets Krishna taught through Sudhama are: selfless action, remembrance at death, non-doership, protection of dharma, and complete surrender. When intellect bows to love, even poison turns to nectar, and destiny itself is rewritten.

Whenever life feels dark, remember Sudhama. Trust Krishna. The pen that rewrites destiny is in your hands—and its ink is faith. If this story moved you, share it with others. May it give you strength in times of hardship. Sarvam Sri Krishnarpanamastu.

types_of_karma.prarabdha_karma: Portion of past karma influencing current life.
